text: The Piasecki VZ-8 Airgeep (company designation PA-59) was a prototype vertical takeoff and landing (VTOL) aircraft developed by Piasecki Aircraft to fulfill a U.S. Army Transportation Research Command contract for a flying jeep in 1957. The design aimed to be smaller and easier to fly than a helicopter. To meet the Army's requirement, Piasecki's aircraft featured two tandem, three-blade ducted rotors, with the crew of two seated between them. Power was provided by two 180 hp (134.2 kW) Lycoming O-360-A2A piston engines, driving the rotors via a central gearbox. The first of two aircraft ordered by the Army, initially called the Model 59K Skycar (later renamed Airgeep) by Piasecki and designated VZ-8P by the Army, made its first flight on 22 September 1958. It was later re-engined with a single 425 hp (317 kW) Turbomeca Artouste IIB turboshaft engine, flying in this configuration in June 1959. After being loaned to the U.S. Navy for evaluation as the Model 59N, where it was fitted with floats, it was returned to the Army and had its engine replaced with a lighter and more powerful 550 hp (410.1 kW) Garrett AiResearch TPE331-6 engine. The second prototype was completed with a modified design, designated Model 59H AirGeep II by Piasecki and VZ-8P (B) by the Army, powered by two Artouste engines, including ejection seats for the pilot and co-pilot/gunner and three additional seats for passengers. It also had a powered tricycle undercarriage to improve land mobility. The AirGeep II's first flight occurred on 15 February 1962, piloted by "Tommy" Atkins. While the Airgeep typically operated close to the ground and could fly to several thousand feet, demonstrating stability in flight and the ability to evade radar detection, the U.S. Army concluded that the "Flying Jeep concept was unsuitable for the modern battlefield" and instead focused on conventional helicopter development, despite its superiority over the other two vehicles evaluated—Chrysler VZ-6 and Curtiss-Wright VZ-7.
